text: A candidate is ahead in the votes counted and released so far. It is not a call and can change as more ballots are counted.
A named news organization has declared a winner based on its own analysis. The dashboard always names who made the call.
The official result after the county canvass and state certification. In Arizona, counties canvass by Nov 19 and the statewide canvass is Nov 23.

AP estimates 'the total votes expected to be cast in any given contest' from past turnout, population change, registration and race competitiveness, and reports the percentage of expected vote counted; that percentage can drop if AP raises its turnout estimate.

topic: Precincts reporting != percent of votes counted
text: Precincts vary in size, and some states report early/mail votes in a single consolidated precinct or exclude them, so a state can show nearly all precincts reporting while many ballots remain uncounted.
AP calls a race only when there is no circumstance in which the trailing candidate can catch up; calls are not projections.

A Decision Team of analysts, researchers and race callers uses the vote count and AP VoteCast; AP 'does not make projections or name apparent or likely winners.' Calls by other organizations have no bearing on AP's timing.

topic: 'Too early to call' / 'too close to call'
text: AP treats races with active, ongoing tabulation as 'too early to call' and has formally declared some races 'too close to call' since 2019; AP may not call a race with a margin under 0.5 percentage points, and may still call a race subject to a possible recount when the lead is large enough.
AP uses about 4,000 stringers to gather local vote totals from county officials; hundreds of vote-entry clerks enter results; automated checks flag anomalies.

Organizations that make race calls include Associated Press (AP), Decision Desk HQ, ABC News decision desk, CBS News decision desk, NBC News decision desk, CNN decision desk, Fox News decision desk. A projection is theirs, not an official result.
